item.title: Establishing Standards for Assessment and Reporting of SNSPD Performance
item.description: arXiv:2611.14653v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPDs) can be made sensitive to single photons with near-unity detection efficiency, ultra-low dark-count rates, and sub-nanosecond timing jitter over a broad wavelength range. However, many studies report data inconsistently, often emphasizing a single performance metric without considering overall device performance. This inconsistent data reporting limits the field, as it makes it difficult to determine which device characteristics are most important. Different applications require functionalities that may conflict with one another; for example, longer-wavelength operation may require lower operating temperatures. Moreover, there is no universally accepted metric for defining the figures of merit of an SNSPD. In this work, we amass a dataset representing the state of the art of SNSPD fabrication, including operating temperature, operating wavelength, photon count rates (PCR), and dark count rates (DCR). We fit the PCR curves and suggest using the saturation plateau length to gauge the SNSPD's sensitivity. We then fit the DCR and compare the PCR and DCR. Using this approach, we establish a quantitative framework to determine the optimal biasing condition for a given device and to determine the device's sensitivity at that optimal biasing condition, enabling meaningful comparisons across disparate devices. Additionally, we offer concrete benchmarks for measuring device performance.

item.title: Development of Sapphire-Based Solid-State Neutron Detectors for Fusion Environments
item.description: arXiv:2611.14745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Single-crystal diamond is the reference solid-state technology for fast neutron detection in fusion devices. Despite this, its complex manufacturing increases their costs and puts limitations on their geometry. Moreover, the limits in their long-term stability and their behaviour in harsh environments further constraint its applications. Synthetic sapphire (Al2O2) is a promising alternative as a solid state detector material: it is available in large, low-cost wafers and features both a wider bandgap and a higher displacement energy compared to diamond. Despite this, it has so far received little-to-no attention as a neutron detector. This work presents the first steps of a development programme for sapphire-based fast neutron detectors. Eight prototypes with 4.5 x 4.5 mm2 and 9 x 9 mm2 active areas and 625 um thickness were fabricated from commercial wafers with Al-Si electrodes and coupled to different electronic configurations. All prototypes detected 5.47 MeV alpha particles from a 241Am source, confirming the viability of both the fabrication process and the use of sapphire as an active material. The small signals (30-40 mV over a peak-to-peak noise of about 8 mV) and the count rate increasing with bias indicate that sapphires will require higher electric fields than the ones experimented in the work (up to about 2.5 kV). Geant4 simulations were also used to estimate the response of a sapphire detector to 14.06 MeV (DT) neutrons, highlighting the perspectives of the detector as a fusion diagnostic.

item.title: The physical design of the superfluid helium-4 UCN source at CSNS
item.description: arXiv:2611.15539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ultracold neutrons (UCN) play a crucial role in fundamental physics research, enabling investigations into new sources of CP violation, neutron lifetime measurements, and the exploration of non-Newtonian forces. However, these experiments are often limited by the intensity of UCN sources. The China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) is developing a UCN source utilizing superfluid helium-4 at Beamline 12. This paper focuses on enhancing UCN density and total UCN number by analyzing various parameters that impact the UCN system, including the influence of different wavelengths of cold neutrons, incident beam size, converter length, wall and reflector materials, extraction method, extraction guide radius, and guide material composition. A preliminary design of the UCN source at CSNS is presented based on this analysis. For a Be-coated converter, the predicted saturated UCN density is 315 UCN/cm^3, with a UCN production rate of 12,055 UCN/s and an extraction efficiency of 84%, yielding approximately 1.3 x 10^6 extracted UCNs per cycle in accumulation mode. The UCN source design presented in this study forms part of the overall physical design of the Neutron Physics and Application Spectrometer at CSNS, which successfully passed its physical design review on March 25, 2025.

item.title: Development of millikelvin scintillation photodetectors with CUPID
item.description: arXiv:2611.15593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CUPID is a next-generation tonne-scale cryogenic experiment that will search for the neutrinoless double beta decay $(0\nu\beta\beta)$ of $^{100}$Mo. It will be located at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Italy) and will employ the cryogenic calorimetric technique to reconstruct the energy deposited in Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ crystals, in which the isotope of interest is embedded. Preliminary measurements have been performed with the CUPID VSTT (Vertical Slice Test Tower), a prototype tower designed to test the detectors' response and the apparatus' mechanical and thermal stability. In addition, a key objective was to demonstrate the improved performance of germanium-based cryogenic light detectors. In CUPID, light detection is used for both particle identification and pile-up rejection. Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ is a scintillating crystal, enabling particle identification by exploiting the dependence of light yield on particle type. This requires collecting the Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillation light, peaking at $\sim$600 nm, with a $\sim$300 $\mu$m-thick high-purity germanium wafer placed next to the crystal. The wafer is also equipped with concentric Al electrodes biased at a few tens of volts. This bias improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude thanks to the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke effect. This work presents preliminary results on the performance of the VSTT light detectors and of its Optical Injection System.

item.title: Xenon energy-deposition widths in silicon: measurements and Geant4 comparisons
item.description: arXiv:2611.15666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Energy-deposition fluctuations determine the isotope-separation capability of multilayer silicon detectors. We measure the central peak widths of $^{124}$Xe signals in 300- and 675-micrometre silicon layers at incident energies of approximately 152-274 MeV per nucleon and compare them with Geant4 11.4.0 electromagnetic option 4 (emopt4) and a calculation with explicit charge exchange. In the 300-micrometre detector, the emopt4 relative width of 1.844% exceeds the unselected experimental width of 1.407% by 31% and the selected width of 1.060% by 74%. For the 675-micrometre detector, selection windows around the downstream-signal peak, each approximately ten fitted first-plane standard deviations wide, give experimental upper estimates of 0.66-0.74%, compared with emopt4 predictions of 1.01-1.24%. Explicit charge-state transport gives widths of 0.889-0.932% for the thinner layer, depending on the incident charge distribution, and 0.59-0.63% for the thicker layer. These predictions are consistent with the experimental upper estimates, while emopt4 overestimates the widths for both thicknesses throughout the studied energy interval.

item.title: Development and characterization of monolithic sensors with internal gain in a 110 nm CMOS process
item.description: arXiv:2611.15731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents the optimization and characterization of a Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor with internal gain implemented in the 110 nm CMOS process from LFoundry. This work, carried out within the framework of the latest ARCADIA production run, reports on the characterization of sensors with an optimized gain layer. Improvements over earlier prototypes, including substrate current reduction via guard-ring connection, are briefly discussed. Both laboratory and in-beam measurements are presented. Using soft X-rays from a 55Fe source, both the pixel response and the noise performance are analyzed. In addition, laser measurements demonstrate an electronic jitter ranging from 20 to 40 ps for a signal amplitude corresponding to one minimum ionizing particle (MIP). Finally, the results from several test beam campaigns are described, showing the signal amplitude, gain and time resolution of sensors with different doping profiles of the gain layer evaluated with MIPs. A time resolution of about 78 ps was measured in the optimal condition of bias voltage and electronics configuration. The results demonstrate that monolithic CMOS sensors with internal gain can achieve promising timing performance at ambient temperature, highlighting their strong potential for next-generation precision timing applications.

item.title: CCGeant4: charge-state-resolved transport and energy-loss fluctuations of relativistic heavy ions in Geant4
item.description: arXiv:2611.15759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: CCGeant4 models energy-loss fluctuations of heavy ions in Geant4, accounting for both charge exchange and relativistic corrections to electron scattering beyond the first Born approximation. We use GLOBAL cross sections for electron capture and loss, ATIMA equilibrium stopping powers and charge-dependent delta-electron spectra calculated from the Dirac equation in a frozen-shell potential. The package also supports tabulated elastic ion-nucleus scattering. The silicon example includes interference between Coulomb and nuclear scattering amplitudes. We compare charge evolution with GLOBAL and energy-loss spectra with MOCADI for matched beams and targets. Experimental comparisons cover the energy-loss measurements of Weick et al. and several measurements of energy deposited by xenon ions in silicon. For uranium at 800 MeV/u, the energy-loss variances from our Dirac configuration agree with the screened-ion calculations of Weick et al. to within 4% in Be, Al and Pb. Both calculations lie within the reported experimental uncertainties for all three targets, while calculated bismuth spectra in silver are narrower than measured. Calculations in thin silicon layers show that delta-electron escape can make deposited-energy distributions substantially narrower than primary-ion energy-loss distributions, highlighting the importance of secondary-electron transport for detector-response modelling. The distribution includes the Geant4 source patch, the transport tables and their converters, and a runnable example.
item.dc:creator: Andrei Azhakin, Ilya Kudryashov

item.title: Characterization of a Large-Area HRPPD MCP-PMT Coupled to LYSO for TOF-PET
item.description: arXiv:2611.15820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-area microchannel-plate photomultipliers (MCP-PMTs) such as the High-Rate Picosecond Photon Detector (HRPPD) are attractive for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). They offer excellent single-photon time resolution, low dark count rate, and large monolithic active areas. However, the coincidence time resolution (CTR) reported so far with PET scintillators falls short of expectations based upon their single-photon time resolution. We characterized a 104x104 mm$^2$ HRPPD coupled to LYSO crystals and read out through a custom high-frequency amplifier. With a 2x2x3 mm$^3$ LYSO crystal we measured a CTR of 107 ps full width at half maximum (FWHM) against a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)-based reference detector. After subtracting the calibrated reference detector's contribution of 42 ps, the single HRPPD detector was found to contribute 98 ps, corresponding to 139 ps for two identical HRPPD detectors in coincidence. With clinical 3x3x20 mm$^3$ crystals the CTR against the reference SiPM detector was 160 ps, corresponding to 218 ps for two identical HRPPD detectors. Timing and gain were uniform across output pads within measurement precision. Summing the four pads under a 3x3x10 mm$^3$ LYSO crystal, the energy resolution for 511 keV gamma ray was 14.6% FWHM, and the 1275 keV line of the $^{22}$Na source was within 1% of its proportional position relative to the 511 keV peak. Flood maps resolved the individual 3 mm elements of a 4x4 array despite the 25 mm pad pitch. To the best of our knowledge the observed timing resolution improves substantially on what has been reported for large-area MCP-PMTs coupled to PET scintillators, and the crystal array identification has not been demonstrated before on such a device. These results indicate that this device class deserves renewed consideration as a photodetector technology for high-performance TOF-PET systems.

item.title: Development and Experimental Characterization of a Compact $^{228}$Th--D$_2$O Photoneutron Source for Low-Energy Nuclear Recoil Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.16415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calibrating the few-keV nuclear-recoil response of liquid xenon detectors calls for a low-energy neutron source. We have developed and characterized a $^{228}$Th--D$_2$O photoneutron source that converts the 2.615~MeV $\gamma$ rays from $^{208}$Tl into sub-MeV neutrons through the D($\gamma$,n)p reaction. After optimizing the D$_2$O geometry to balance neutron production against escape efficiency, we validated the chosen configuration experimentally. The forward emission rate is $1734 \pm 76~(\mathrm{stat.}) \pm 65~(\mathrm{sys.})~\mathrm{h}^{-1}$, and the spectrum unfolded from Bonner sphere data is concentrated at $0.17$--$0.22~\mathrm{MeV}$. In a 220~h exposure of PandaX-20T, the same configuration should provide about 1000 selected nuclear-recoil events. These results support the use of a long-lived $^{228}$Th--D$_2$O source for low-energy neutron calibration of large liquid xenon detectors.

item.title: Progress on the MALTA CMOS Sensor: Edge-TCT Measurements for Parametric Pixel Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: MALTA2 is a monolithic active pixel sensor, developed in the 180 nm CMOS imaging technology for radiation-hard applications in high-rate environments. This contribution summarizes recent developments in the characterization and simulation of MALTA2. The charge collection of a sensor on epitaxial silicon is studied with the Edge Transient Current Technique (Edge-TCT), using a digital readout, where the charge is reconstructed solely from binary hit data. In previous works, only specially designed analog output pixels at the matrix periphery were investigated. In contrast, the digital readout gives access to the full edge of the pixel matrix. Laser scans across neighboring pixels enable a two-dimensional parameterization of the charge collection. This parameterization serves as input to a parametric pixel simulation, which has been developed for chip design optimization and system-level studies. The simulation results are validated with test beam data.

item.title: Development of a Cryogenic Anti-Coincidence System Based on Scintillating Crystals Read Out with Kinetic Inductance Detectors for BULLKID-DM
item.description: arXiv:2611.17089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The BULLKID-DM experiment has been proposed to search for WIMP-like dark matter particles with a mass of 1 GeV or lower and with a WIMP-nucleon interaction cross section down to $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$. To achieve this goal, the experiment utilizes a detector consisting of a stack of 16 silicon wafers instrumented with phonon-mediated superconducting Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs), to be operated at the underground facility of the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), Italy. To reduce the residual background arising from $\gamma$-rays, neutrons, and muons, a cryogenic active anti-coincidence system (veto) operating at mK temperature, surrounding the main detector, is under development. The veto detector consists of segmented scintillating crystals read out by phonon-mediated KID light detectors. Current status and future developments of the veto system are presented. In particular, we focus on cryogenic tests of both bismuth germanate (BGO) and gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) crystals, which had been previously chosen as veto candidate crystals according to our preliminary studies on the dependence of their optical properties (i.e. light yield and scintillation decay time) on temperature. We finally present the operation and preliminary tests of a two-module veto prototype with multiplexed readout.

item.title: Adaptive carrier signal synthesis for frequency-division multiplexed cryogenic detector readout
item.description: arXiv:2611.17099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frequency-domain multiplexing is a fundamental technology for readout of cryogenic detector arrays on a single transmission line. Synthesizing a large number of static carrier tones for resonator stimulation eventually drives the cryogenic low-noise amplifier beyond its P1dB, introducing detector signal distortion. Scaling array sizes to O(10^6) detector pixels therefore demands minimizing the total power on the transmission line by continuous tracking of the resonances, which requires the readout electronics to be capable of updating the carrier tones dynamically. This work presents an scalable FPGA-based implementation for carrier signal synthesis based on a numerically controlled oscillator and a polyphase filter bank, enabling real-time frequency adaptivity as well as frequency resolution of 4 mHz to precisely tune the operating point, while simultaneously reducing resource usage compared to the current memory-based implementation.

item.title: The Gator low-background spectrometer: readout upgrade and photomultiplier tube radioassay for XLZD
item.description: arXiv:2611.17187v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on a readout upgrade of Gator, a low-background high-purity germanium spectrometer operated at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso for material radioassay. The upgraded data acquisition records digitised waveforms, enabling noise rejection on an event-level basis, and offline energy reconstruction. Measurements before and after the upgrade show an improved energy resolution of 17% at the 2614.5 keV line of 208-Tl, with (2.14 +- 0.22) keV at FWHM, and suppression of electronic noise in the low-energy region. We assess the resulting sensitivity for a specified sample geometry, and present a new background measurement. The background rate in the (100-2700) keV range is (86.6 +- 0.5) counts/(kg day). We also show the radioassay results of sixteen Hamamatsu R17317 3-inch photomultiplier tubes with an improved stem design, which reduces the activities from the primordial 238-U and 232-Th chains by a factor of three, making them suitable candidate photosensors for the XLZD experiment.
item.dc:creator: Laura Baudis, Sofia Calgaro, Jose Javier Cuenca-Garcia, Florian Joerg, Margherita Noia, Francesco Piastra, Aravind Remesan Sreekala

item.title: Subpicosecond Optical Time Transfer under Simulated Motion with Electro-Optic Frequency Combs
item.description: arXiv:2611.15763v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Extension of high performance optical frequency comb-based time transfer to real-world systems is challenged by platform motion, particularly for large relative velocities. Here, we utilize agile electro-optic frequency combs to construct a laboratory-based simulator of a two-way optical time transfer system under motion. Through direct control of the electro-optic frequency comb parameters, we can artificially induce the effects of relative motion. We performed tests of the time transfer performance across a km-scale fiber link for velocity profiles that linearly increase from rest up to 400 m/s. Through a post-processed data analysis, we demonstrate continuous tracking of the clock offset between sites with subpicosecond precision throughout the velocity sweep. These results illustrate the versatility of using electro-optic frequency combs for optical time transfer in deployed systems.
item.dc:creator: Nolan Matthews, Joshua Olson, Robert Rockmore, Sean Krzyzewski

item.title: SimpleClock: a satellite-disciplined oscillator for astronomical instrumentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.16023v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: SimpleClock is a low-cost, high-stability timing reference designed for astronomical experiments that combines a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) timing receiver, a digitally tunable 10 MHz microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) oven-controlled oscillator, external thermal regulation and autonomous control. It provides 10 MHz and pulse-per-second references at an estimated prototype hardware cost of US\$500. Independently enabled frequency and phase feedback support precise point positioning (PPP) with Galileo's High Accuracy Service (HAS), satellite-based augmentation system (SBAS) solutions and standalone operation. Three-unit phase comparisons separate component noise and characterize disciplined-output stability over 200\,000 s recordings. Across five configurations, each analysed over 200\,000 s, equivalent single-unit differential Allan deviation and time deviation at 1000 s span $3.5\times10^{-13}$--$1.0\times10^{-12}$ and 115--447 ps, respectively. The maximum equivalent time deviation over averaging times from 1 to 50\,000 s spans 143--1090 ps. These results support applications in astronomical timing, including low-frequency very long baseline interferometry (VLBI).
item.dc:creator: Albert Wai Kit Lau, Bruno Pollarolo, Juan Mena-Parra

item.title: Crest factor optimization of multi-tone signals generated for low-temperature sensor readout
item.description: arXiv:2611.17207v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKID) are a growing technology of cryogenic detectors and have a great potential in radio-astronomy and cosmic microwave background (CMB) characterization. A review of the general readout performance requirements for experiments requiring the multiplexing of large arrays (~10.000 pixels) of such cryogenic detectors is presented. The focus is on the crest factor optimization process for proper excitation and readout of these large arrays of detectors. It is shown an algorithm to optimize the phase generation of the carriers to obtain a low crest factor, favoring the dynamic range usage of the electronic chain.
item.dc:creator: L. H. Arnaldi

item.title: Machine learning methods for subpixel trajectory reconstruction in discretized position detectors
item.description: arXiv:2512.20645v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We evaluate machine-learning methods for sub-pixel position and trajectory-angle reconstruction in scintillator detectors. Geant4 simulations use two $50 \times 50$ cm plastic-scintillator planes separated by 30 cm, each represented by an $8 \times 8$ grid of 64 touching computational cells of pitch 6.25 cm. The plates are optically continuous. Photons reaching any outer face are absorbed and scored once in the pre-step cell. We sum the collected photon energies in each cell and normalize the signals to the plane total. Photodetectors and electronics are not simulated. We compare a transformer, a convolutional neural network (CNN), a multilayer perceptron (MLP), and an energy-weighted centroid. We compute directions from the two reconstructed positions. On a common 19,053-event test set, transformer and CNN median position errors (per-event means of the two planes' radial errors) are 0.18 and 0.23 cm, or 2.9% and 3.6% of the cell width. Their median space-angle errors are $0.35^\circ$ and $0.52^\circ$, compared with 1.03 cm and $1.90^\circ$ for the centroid and $4.21^\circ$ for an idealized Monte Carlo reference retaining only the traversed cell. The transformer has the lowest median errors, whereas the CNN has the lowest position- and angular-RMSE point estimates. Large-error tails limit the RMSE gains. Learned methods recover sub-pixel information in this idealized response. Establishing gains for muon tomography requires realistic optical coupling, photodetector response, and electronics.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Mark Romano, Zhengzhi Liu, JungHyun Bae

item.title: Physics at the Edge: Benchmarking Quantisation Techniques and the Edge TPU for Neutrino Interaction Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2603.24607v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work presents a benchmark of quantisation techniques for convolutional neural networks applied to neutrino interaction recognition, motivated by the need for low-power inference close to the detector in future liquid argon time-projection chamber (LArTPC) experiments. Using simulation of a generic LArTPC, four Keras models are trained to classify neutral-current, muon-neutrino charged-current and electron-neutrino charged-current interactions, quantised using post-training integer quantisation and quantisation-aware training, and deployed on the Google Coral Edge TPU. Latency and energy per event are compared with those of an Intel Core i7-13650HX CPU, a consumer NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU and a data-centre NVIDIA A100 GPU, using measured energy at different batch sizes and thread counts; the energy of the Edge TPU is estimated from its nominal power. The accuracy degradation is strongly model-dependent: InceptionV3 shows no significant loss along either pipeline, whereas the other models are substantially degraded. At batch size 1, the Edge TPU is comparable to or faster than the CPU and 1.3-6.5 times slower than the A100, while requiring 5--70 times less energy per event than the other devices; with batching, the GPUs reduce this gap to a factor of 2.6-7.2. The Edge TPU is also approximately four times cheaper than the consumer GPU and more than two orders of magnitude cheaper than the A100. Its low power per device eases deployment where power and cooling are constrained, with an additional benefit in terms of environmental impact. This paper explores possible future integrations of edge AI technologies with neutrino physics.
item.dc:creator: Stefano Vergani, Hilary Utaegbulam, Michael Wang, Leigh H. Whitehead, Arden S. H. Tsang, Lorenzo Uboldi

item.title: Operation and performance of ProtoDUNE Dual Phase liquid argon time projection chamber
item.description: arXiv:2607.15927v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ProtoDUNE-DP, with a total mass of the active volume of 300 t, is the largest Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) built to operate in a Dual-Phase (DP) mode where the ionisation charge produced in the liquid bulk by charged particles traversing the detector is transferred for the readout in the gaseous phase above. Intended as a prototype of a far detector module for the DUNE neutrino oscillation experiment, ProtoDUNE-DP was operated at the CERN Neutrino Platform from 2019 to 2022. This paper describes various ProtoDUNE-DP detector components, discusses the commissioning and operation experiences, and presents the results on the detector performance from an analysis of collected cosmic ray data. Some key deliverables of the detector were achieved, including stable delivery of 300 kV to the TPC cathode, operation of the charge readout with an effective gain exceeding 5 before charging-up, stable functioning of the photon detection system with a relative time accuracy among PMTs below 16 ns. The long term operation of the charge readout system in dual-phase, however, was limited by the liquid surface and electrical instabilities. The ProtoDUNE-DP experience contributed to the final design of the DUNE Vertical Drift LArTPC.

item.title: Multi-Angle Beam Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy for Diffraction-Contrast-Free Magnetic Imaging
item.description: arXiv:2609.03303v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent development of the differential phase contrast (DPC) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) technique has significantly advanced materials science supported by high-sensitivity detectors and powerful data processing. Especially the 4D-STEM technique, employing a pixelated camera as a STEM detector, enables extensive information acquisition through post-processing of large datasets. However, magnetic or electric field imaging using DPC is often disturbed by diffraction contrasts intrinsic to the crystalline material. In this paper, we demonstrate elimination of the diffraction contrasts for magnetic field imaging by using angularly distributed multiple electron beams generated by a multi-hole aperture within the 4D-STEM framework. This multi-angle beam configuration suppresses irrelevant crystalline contrast and yields direct magnetic information with high sensitivity from the specimen. The resulting 4D-STEM datasets also enable additional analysis of sub-beam size magnetic domain structures, domain walls, and diffraction-related information.
item.dc:creator: Akira Yasuhara, Zentaro Akase, Takumi Sannomiya

item.title: Imaging performance of a Single-Plane Readout Compton Camera
item.description: arXiv:2609.20841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work presents the design, development, and characterization of a compact Compton camera employing a novel single-plane readout architecture. The proposed concept simplifies conventional multilayer Compton cameras by optically coupling the scatterer and absorber into a single compact detector element using a light guide, enabling readout exclusively from one side with silicon photomultipliers. The system was validated through Monte Carlo simulations, prototype construction, and experimental characterization using standard gamma-ray sources. Detector performance for 511~keV and 662~keV photons was optimized using simulations based on the Geant4 framework, by guiding event selection strategy. Event reconstruction relied on coincidence detection consistent with Compton scattering kinematics, while image reconstruction was performed using maximum likelihood expectation maximization algorithm. The prototype comprises 64 detector elements arranged in an $8\times8$ matrix, read out by an $8\times8$ silicon photomultiplier array. Each element consists of two GAGG:Ce scintillators coupled by a 20 mm long light guide. Measured energy resolutions were $8.9\%\pm1.9\%$ and $10.8\%\pm1.6\%$ for the front and back layers, respectively. Successful gamma-ray imaging was demonstrated for Na-22 and Cs-137 sources, achieving angular resolutions of $12.4^\circ$--$14.3^\circ$ at 511~keV and $14.3^\circ$--$16.8^\circ$ at 662~keV, confirming the feasibility of the proposed single-plane architecture for compact and cost-effective gamma-ray imaging applications.

item.title: Track fitting at the full LHC collision rate
item.description: arXiv:2607.14793v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The LHCb experiment at the Large Hadron Collider underwent a major upgrade before the LHC Run 3 data-taking period, employing an all-software approach in its trigger system. Here we present a fast implementation of a Kalman filter, used in the first trigger stage since the 2025 data-taking period, allowing to determine parameter estimates of charged-particle trajectories at the full LHCb collision frequency of 30 MHz. This approach replaces computationally expensive magnetic field map lookups and numerical integration methods with fast analytical parameterisations while maintaining the mathematical framework of Kalman filtering. Implemented on approximately 500 GPUs within the first-level trigger, the algorithm has replaced the previous partial track fitting algorithm in the real-time trigger environment at the cost of a 2% increase in processing time. Compared to the previous fitter this parameterised Kalman filter shows a significantly improved momentum resolution, resulting in a factor of two improvement in the invariant mass resolutions for reconstructed D0 and J/{\psi} hadrons. It additionally demonstrates greater robustness against detector misalignment effects and substantially sharpens the discrimination between genuine particle trajectories and accidental background, more than doubling the rejection of the latter at no cost to genuine-track efficiency, for a standard selection working point.
item.dc:creator: Pierre Billoir, Thomas Boettcher, Michel De Cian, Lennart H. Uecker

item.title: GeoRead: Geometry-Aware Transformer for Continuous AC-LGAD Readout Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.08694v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: AC-coupled Low-Gain Avalanche Diodes (AC-LGADs) are promising silicon sensor technologies for high-precision four-dimensional tracking. Position reconstruction in AC-LGADs relies on correlations among waveforms induced on multiple readout pads, where analytically solving the signal propagation becomes difficult, motivating data-based machine learning reconstruction. Existing machine learning approaches generally assume a fixed readout pad layout and predict one hit from an isolated, temporally aligned waveform window. These assumptions limit their flexibility across sensor designs and applicability to continuous readout where signal arrival times are not known in advance and multiple hits might overlap in the same waveforms. We introduce GeoRead, a spatial-temporal Transformer enabling multi-event continuous position prediction and uncertainty estimation. We incorporate relative pad positions into attention and produces time-resolved hit position estimates with predictive uncertainties. Time-jitter and additive event-mixing augmentations are used to train the model on temporally misaligned and overlapping waveforms synthesized from single-event measurements. Using four-channel transient-current-technique (TCT) data of a 500\mum-pitch AC-LGAD, GeoRead achieves median position errors of 5.8\mum within the convex hull of the readout-pad centers and 8.2\mum over the full scanned region at 190\volt. The model maintains comparable accuracy under temporal shifts and demonstrates time-resolved reconstruction of superposed events, without predefined per-event window. These results provide a basis for extending waveform-based position reconstruction toward continuous readout and flexible sensor geometries.
